section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Distribution
section_1.content: Briefly review that a distribution is a way of showing how data is spread out. Introduce the 'Uniform Distribution' (where all outcomes are equally likely) as our starting point.
section_1.example: Imagine a fair 6-sided die. Rolling it once gives a flat, uniform distribution of outcomes (1 through 6).

section_2.title: The Hook: The Chaos of One vs. The Order of Many
section_2.content: Pose the question: What happens if we take multiple samples and calculate their average? Visually contrast a single sample's distribution with the distribution of the 'mean of samples'.
section_2.example: If you roll one die, the result is random. If you roll 50 dice and take their average, the result will almost always be close to 3.5. Why does the chaos vanish?

section_3.title: Core Concept: The Normal Approximation
section_3.content: Define the CLT: As the sample size (n) increases, the distribution of sample means approaches a Normal Distribution (Bell Curve), regardless of the shape of the original population distribution.
section_3.example: Visual animation: Start with a wildly skewed 'Exponential' distribution. As we increase the number of items being averaged (n=2, n=5, n=30), the graph morphs in real-time into a smooth, symmetrical bell curve.

section_4.title: Visualizing the Bell Curve
section_4.content: Highlight the two key parameters that emerge from the CLT: the mean of the sample means (which equals the population mean) and the shrinking variance (standard error).
section_4.example: Show a 'Galton Board' animation where thousands of marbles bounce through pegs; even though each marble's path is random, they pile up to form a perfect bell curve.

section_5.title: Application: Real-World Predictability
section_5.content: Explain why this is powerful: The CLT allows us to make predictions about populations even when we don't know the original distribution shape. It is the bridge between sample data and population inference.
section_5.example: A delivery robot company measures battery life. Even if individual battery failures are unpredictable, the average battery life of a large fleet follows a predictable bell curve, allowing the company to guarantee delivery times.

                           "Many samples averaged become predictable."])
        
        # Define elements
        particle = Dot(color="#FF4500", radius=0.1)
        particles = VGroup(*[Dot(color="#FF4500", radius=0.05) for _ in range(100)])
        wave = FunctionGraph(lambda x: 0.5 * np.sin(3 * x), x_range=[-1.5, 1.5], color="#00FF00")

        self.place_at_grid(particle, 'C3')
        self.play(FadeIn(particle))
        self.play(particle.animate.shift(UP * 0.5), run_time=0.5)
        self.play(particle.animate.shift(LEFT * 0.5), run_time=0.5)
        self.play(particle.animate.shift(DOWN * 0.8), run_time=0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Color line
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FF4500"))
        # Animation: Populate screen
        for p in particles:
            self.place_in_area(p, 'B4', 'E6')
        self.play(LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(p) for p in particles], lag_ratio=0.01))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Color line
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))
        # Animation: Smooth movement
        self.place_in_area(wave, 'B4', 'E6')
        self.play(FadeOut(particles), FadeIn(wave))
        self.play(wave.animate.set_stroke(width=4), run_time=2)
